concepts.def: Northern Ireland Prime Minister 1963-69 who pursued modernisation and met Irish Taoiseach Seán Lemass in 1965, but his cautious reforms angered hard-line unionists while disappointing nationalists.
From 1967 NICRA campaigned against discrimination in housing allocation, jobs and local government voting; marches from 1968 met violence and escalated tensions.
Roughly thirty years of conflict from the late 1960s involving republican and loyalist paramilitaries and the security forces, killing around 3,500 people.
On 30 January 1972 British paratroopers shot dead thirteen civil rights marchers in Derry/Londonderry; Stormont was suspended and direct rule from London followed.
Deal signed by Thatcher and FitzGerald giving the Republic of Ireland a consultative role in Northern Ireland affairs, provoking mass unionist protest under the slogan 'Ulster Says No'.
April 1998 settlement creating a power-sharing Assembly, North-South bodies and the principle of consent, endorsed by referendums on both sides of the border.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Changing Relations: Northern Ireland & its Neighbours 1965-98 — a core area of GCSE History.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Changing Relations: Northern Ireland & its Neighbours 1965-98 brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Changing Relations: Northern Ireland & its Neighbours 1965-98.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What did the Good Friday Agreement of 1998 establish?
options: A power-sharing Assembly and the principle that Northern Ireland's status can only change by consent
Immediate Irish unification
Permanent direct rule from London
A new border between Belfast and Derry

mcqs.q: What happened on Bloody Sunday, 30 January 1972?
options: British paratroopers shot dead thirteen civil rights marchers in Derry/Londonderry
The IRA bombed Belfast city centre
The Good Friday Agreement was signed
Stormont was restored to full power

mcqs.q: What did NICRA campaign for from 1967?
options: Equal rights in housing, jobs and local government voting within Northern Ireland
An immediate united Ireland
The closure of the border with the Republic
Withdrawal of Northern Ireland from the United Nations

mcqs.q: Why did unionists protest against the Anglo-Irish Agreement of 1985?
options: It gave the Dublin government a consultative role in Northern Ireland without unionist consent
It abolished the Northern Ireland border immediately
It banned all unionist political parties
It removed British troops overnight

mcqs.q: What did the civil rights movement of the late 1960s actually demand?
options: The Agreement removed Northern Ireland from the United Kingdom.
NICRA campaigned mainly for women's right to vote in Westminster elections.
Equal treatment for all citizens within Northern Ireland — fair housing allocation, an end to gerrymandering and 'one man, one vote' in local elections.
NICRA was simply a front organisation demanding an immediate united Ireland.

mcqs.q: What happened on Bloody Sunday in 1972?
options: British soldiers shot dead thirteen civil rights marchers in Derry/Londonderry on 30 January 1972; a fourteenth victim died later.
Bloody Sunday was a gun battle between rival paramilitary groups in Dublin.
Bloody Sunday was the IRA bombing of Belfast city centre.
NICRA campaigned mainly for women's right to vote in Westminster elections.

mcqs.q: Did the Good Friday Agreement instantly end all violence?
options: NICRA campaigned mainly for women's right to vote in Westminster elections.
The 1998 Agreement immediately stopped all paramilitary activity.
It created the political framework that largely ended the conflict, but violence did not vanish — the Omagh bomb came in August 1998 and decommissioning disputes dragged on for years.
The Agreement removed Northern Ireland from the United Kingdom.
